title: Group employees by department but return the result as a `TreeMap` so the department keys are sorted alphabetically, using the three-argument `Collectors.groupingBy`. Explain how to choose the map implementation and the downstream collector.
shortTitle: Group employees by department into a sorted TreeMap using groupingBy with a map supplier

s1_definition.profdef: The three-argument `Collectors.groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream)` groups elements by a classifier function, stores the groups in a map created by the supplied factory (for example `TreeMap::new` for sorted keys), and reduces each group with the downstream collector (for example `toList()`). The default two-argument form uses a `HashMap`, which has no key order.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya sorts employee files into labelled trays by department. The ordinary way throws the trays on the shelf in no order (HashMap). The sorted way (TreeMap) keeps the trays in alphabetical order by department label, so Risk comes after Management automatically.
s1_definition.oneliner: `groupingBy(classifier, TreeMap::new, downstream)` groups into a map whose keys are kept sorted, instead of the unordered default HashMap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The three-argument `Collectors.groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream)` groups elements by a classifier function, stores the groups in a map created by the supplied factory (for example `TreeMap::new` for sorted keys), and reduces each group with the downstream collector (for example `toList()`). The default two-argument form uses a `HashMap`, which has no key order.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya sorts employee files into labelled trays by department. The ordinary way throws the trays on the shelf in no order (HashMap). The sorted way (TreeMap) keeps the trays in alphabetical order by department label, so Risk comes after Management automatically.

**One line to remember:** `groupingBy(classifier, TreeMap::new, downstream)` groups into a map whose keys are kept sorted, instead of the unordered default HashMap.

sections.s2_technical:
`groupingBy` has three overloads. The one-argument form `groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment)` returns `Map<String, List<Employee>>` backed by a HashMap. The two-argument form adds a downstream collector, like `groupingBy(dept, counting())`. The three-argument form inserts a map factory in the middle: `groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, TreeMap::new, toList())` returns a `TreeMap<String, List<Employee>>` whose keys are sorted by their natural order.

A worked finance example: to list employees per department with departments displayed alphabetically, `employees.stream().collect(groupingBy(Employee::getDepartment, TreeMap::new, toList()))`. The TreeMap keeps Management before Risk before Settlement before Trading without any extra sort step.

The senior nuance is that you choose the map factory to match your need: TreeMap for sorted keys (optionally with a custom comparator via `() -> new TreeMap<>(comparator)`), LinkedHashMap to preserve encounter order of first appearance, or the default HashMap for best throughput when order does not matter. The downstream collector is fully composable, so you can combine sorting of keys with counting, averaging, or mapping of the grouped values.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's org-chart screen lists employees grouped by department, and the departments must appear in alphabetical order so the page is predictable and easy to scan. A plain groupingBy returns a HashMap whose key order is arbitrary, which makes the screen jumble departments differently on each run.

This is exactly why the three-argument groupingBy with TreeMap::new exists — it groups by department and stores the groups in a TreeMap, so the department keys stay sorted alphabetically with no extra work.

The code defines `Employee`, an `OrgChartService.byDepartmentSorted` method, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: five employees across Trading, Risk, Management, and Settlement.

Step 1: The classifier reads each employee's department as the grouping key.

Step 2: The TreeMap factory creates a map that keeps keys sorted by natural String order as entries are inserted.

Step 3: The mapping downstream collects only the names into each group's list.

Step 4: The finished TreeMap holds Management, Risk, Settlement, Trading in that alphabetical order.

Step 5: Iterating the TreeMap yields departments alphabetically, so the org-chart screen is stable.

```
INFO: Management -> [Vikram]
INFO: Risk -> [Priya]
INFO: Settlement -> [Amit]
INFO: Trading -> [Rajesh, Sneha]
```

```
    │ groupingBy(dept, TreeMap::new, mapping(name, toList))
    ▼
  TreeMap (keys sorted on insert):
    Management → [Vikram]
    Risk       → [Priya]
    Settlement → [Amit]
    Trading    → [Rajesh, Sneha]

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
groupingBy has three overloads, and the three-argument form is the one I reach for when I care about the type and ordering of the result map. It takes the classifier that decides the key, a map factory that chooses the map implementation, and a downstream collector that reduces each group. By passing TreeMap new as the factory I get a map whose department keys are kept sorted in natural order, instead of the arbitrary order of the default HashMap.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India the org-chart screen grouped employees by department and had to show departments alphabetically so the page looked the same on every load. I used groupingBy with the department as the classifier, TreeMap new as the factory, and a mapping downstream that collected just the employee names, and the result came out already sorted by department without any separate sort step.

The senior point I always add is that the map factory is a deliberate design choice. TreeMap gives sorted keys and can take a custom comparator, LinkedHashMap preserves the order in which keys first appear, and the default HashMap gives the best throughput when order does not matter. Because the downstream collector is fully composable, I can combine sorted keys with counting, averaging, or mapping in the same call.
